question: What main body part does a doctor look at during a laryngoscopy?
explanation: Spot on! Laryngoscopy is all about checking out the larynx and vocal cords so doctors can see what's happening or help with breathing tubes. You've got this! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is a laryngoscopy done?

options.A: It takes X-rays of the chest and inflates collapsed lung tissue simultaneously.
options.B: It measures blood pressure in the throat and delivers emergency oral medications.
options.C: It cures chronic lung infections and removes foreign bodies from the stomach.
options.D: It checks voice box issues and also helps place breathing tubes during resuscitation.

explanation: Exactly! It's a handy tool both for figuring out throat problems and for guiding breathing tubes when someone needs emergency help. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which of these is a common reason a patient would need a laryngoscopy?
explanation: Well done! If someone's voice has been unusually rough or hoarse for a long time, doctors use a laryngoscopy to take a closer look at the vocal cords. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h2)

question: A patient swallowed a small toy that got stuck in their throat. Why would a doctor perform a laryngoscopy?

options.A: To test the patient's swallowing reflex
options.B: To locate and safely remove the inhaled object
options.C: To measure the oxygen content in the lungs
options.D: To check for chronic bacterial throat infections

explanation: Spot on! When something gets stuck where it shouldn't be, this procedure lets the clinician spot the object and safely take it out. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h2)

question: What do we call the type of laryngoscopy that uses a thin, flexible camera passed through the nose?
explanation: You got it! A fiberoptic scope uses a flexible, thin camera that slides easily through the nose while the patient is awake. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is a big plus of using a flexible fiberoptic scope instead of a rigid one in the clinic?

options.A: The patient can remain awake and talk while vocal cord movement is assessed.
options.B: It completely eliminates any risk of a patient gagging during the test.
options.C: It provides a wider surgical field for removing large vocal cord tumors.
options.D: It requires full general anesthesia to relax the throat muscles completely.

explanation: Exactly! Because the patient is awake, doctors can actually watch how the vocal cords move when they talk or breathe. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h3)

question: As a nurse, what is a crucial check to perform on a direct laryngoscope before the procedure starts?

options.A: Testing the light source to ensure the bulb works
options.B: Filling the battery compartment with sterile water
options.C: Calibrating the internal digital video monitor
options.D: Sterilizing the handle in a high-heat autoclave

explanation: Great job! You always want to make sure the light is working brightly before the doctor tries to look into the airway. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why do doctors often use numbing spray and a nasal decongestant before a flexible scope goes into the nose?

options.A: To numb the passage, reduce discomfort, and shrink mucosal tissues for easier scope entry
options.B: To dilate the pupils so the patient can see the monitor during the examination
options.C: To put the patient into a deep sleep and prevent sudden body movements
options.D: To relax the heart rate and lower the patient's resting blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! The nose and throat are very sensitive, so numbing and shrinking the tissues makes the scope slide in much more comfortably. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why must a nurse check that a patient hasn't eaten or drunk anything (NPO status) before a scheduled laryngoscopy?

options.A: To allow the doctor to take accurate tissue biopsy samples
options.B: To prevent allergic reactions to the topical anesthetic spray
options.C: To minimize the risk of aspiration if sedation or local numbing is used
options.D: To ensure the patient's blood pressure remains stable throughout the test

explanation: You nailed it! Numbing the throat turns off the gag reflex for a bit, so fasting keeps food or drink from accidentally slipping into the lungs. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h5)

question: A patient is scared they will suffocate when the scope goes into their nose. How should you, as the nurse, respond?

options.A: Inform them that the procedure will be canceled until their anxiety goes away completely.
options.B: Tell them to hold their breath entirely until the doctor pulls the camera back out.
options.C: Assure them that a breathing machine will completely take over their lungs during the procedure.
options.D: Explain that they will still be able to breathe freely through their nose and mouth around the thin scope.

explanation: Wonderful nursing care! Reassuring patients that the scope is tiny and their airway is wide open does wonders to calm their nerves. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which vital sign must you keep a close eye on continuously during a laryngoscopy?
explanation: Spot on! Because we are working right in the airway, watching oxygen levels closely ensures the patient is getting enough air the whole time. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h6)

question: During a laryngoscopy, a patient's oxygen level suddenly drops from 98% to 85%. What is your immediate action as the nurse?

options.A: Administer an oral pain medication to relax the vocal cords.
options.B: Document the drop in the chart and wait for the doctor to finish looking.
options.C: Alert the clinician, stop the procedure, and provide supplemental oxygen or bag-valve-mask ventilation.
options.D: Ask the patient to sit up straight and take three deep breaths through their mouth.

explanation: Safety first! A sudden drop in oxygen means you must stop what's happening right away, get help, and give the patient oxygen. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main thing you must check before letting a patient drink water after a throat-numbing laryngoscopy?

options.A: The passage of urine into the bedside commode
options.B: A stable body temperature for two hours
options.C: The return of the gag reflex and swallowing ability
options.D: A completely normal blood pressure reading

explanation: You got it! Always wait for the numbing medicine to wear off and the gag reflex to come back so they don't choke or aspirate water. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why should you tell a patient to avoid clearing their throat aggressively right after a laryngoscopy?

options.A: It prevents the doctor from writing the final discharge summary.
options.B: It increases the patient's blood pressure and heart rate significantly.
options.C: It forces the residual topical spray down into the stomach too fast.
options.D: It can cause trauma or irritation to the recently numbed vocal cords.

explanation: Spot on! Since the vocal cords are still a bit sleepy and vulnerable, harsh throat clearing can easily bruise or injure them. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h7)

question: What do we call a sudden, involuntary spasm of the vocal cords that blocks a patient's airway?
explanation: Brilliant! A laryngospasm is when the vocal cords suddenly clamp shut, making it hard to breathe and needing quick action. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT something you should do when managing a sudden laryngospasm?

options.A: Calling for immediate medical assistance and emergency help
options.B: Applying 100% oxygen via a face mask or bag-valve-mask
options.C: Administering a large volume of ice-cold water by mouth
options.D: Ensuring the patient's airway remains open and unobstructed

explanation: You nailed it! Never give water by mouth when someone is having an airway spasm or can't swallow properly—that's a major choking hazard. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T4#GNS221_U2_T4_h8)
